topic: When the same money buys less
headline_fact: When prices rise faster than your budget, the same money buys fewer goods.
summary: A simple basket example explains purchasing power without treating one price change as a measure of all inflation.
did_you_know: A budget and the prices of goods work together to determine what you can buy.
core_mechanics: The quantity a fixed budget can buy falls when the price per unit rises.
why_it_matters: Money has meaning through the goods and services it can buy.

in_depth_breakdown.real_world_application: Comparing the same basket makes a change in purchasing power easier to see.

learning_takeaways: Purchasing power describes what money can buy.
A fixed budget buys fewer unchanged goods when their price rises.
One basket example does not measure all inflation.

identity.name: When the same money buys less
identity.scope: A fixed budget and one unchanged basket of goods
identity.geography: An illustrative shopping example, not a country-wide price measure

economics_lesson.hook: When prices rise faster than your budget, the same money buys fewer goods.
economics_lesson.question: Why can the same ₹500 buy less than before?
economics_lesson.learning_goal: Explain purchasing power through a fixed budget and a changing basket price.

opening_scenario.title: The budget stays the same. The basket gets smaller.
opening_scenario.experience: You set aside ₹500 for a weekly shop. The same basket used to cost ₹100, but now costs ₹125. You still hold ₹500. What changes is the quantity it can buy.
opening_scenario.question: What does your money buy now?

economics_lesson.central_idea: The quantity a fixed budget can buy falls when the price per unit rises. Purchasing power means the goods and services that an amount of money can buy.

key_terms.meaning: The goods and services that an amount of money can buy.
A measure that combines prices across a defined set of goods and services. One basket example alone does not establish a change in a whole economy.

actors.name: The shopper
actors.role: Chooses how to use a fixed budget.

actors.name: The seller
actors.role: Offers the same basket at the stated price.

steps.title: Start with a fixed budget
steps.action: The shopper sets aside ₹500. For this example, the budget does not change.
steps.what_changes: The spending limit is held constant so we can study the effect of a price change.
steps.why_next: A fixed amount of money buys a quantity that depends on the price per basket.

steps.title: The price per basket rises
steps.action: The basket price changes from ₹100 to ₹125. Its contents and quality stay the same.
steps.what_changes: Each basket takes a larger part of the budget.
steps.why_next: With a fixed budget, a higher price leaves room for fewer baskets.
conditions: The basket has the same contents and quality.
This example does not explain why the seller changes the price.

steps.title: The budget buys fewer baskets
steps.action: The shopper can buy four baskets at ₹125 each instead of five at ₹100 each.
steps.what_changes: Purchasing power over this basket falls, even though the amount of money stays the same.
steps.why_next: The comparison separates the money amount from the quantity that it can buy.
conditions: There are no discounts, substitutions, fees or changes in income.

worked_example.title: Follow a ₹500 shopping budget

provenance.description: Invented numbers explain a fixed budget. They do not describe measured prices.

assumptions: Each basket contains the same goods in the same quantities.
The shopper can buy complete baskets without extra charges.

calculations.label: Baskets before the price change
calculations.explanation: Divide the budget by the price of one basket: ₹500 buys five baskets.

calculations.label: Baskets after the price change
calculations.explanation: The same calculation with the later price gives four baskets.

reasoning: Keep the budget and basket contents unchanged.
Compare the quantities that the budget buys at each price.
worked_example.outcome: The budget buys one fewer basket.
worked_example.explanation: The amount of money stays at ₹500, but its purchasing power over this basket falls.
limits: This example does not measure economy-wide inflation.
Real shoppers can change products, quantities or shops.

diagram.title: Same budget, fewer baskets
diagram.caption: Both bars start at zero. The values are illustrative, not observed price data.
diagram.description: At the earlier price, ₹500 buys five baskets. At the later price, it buys four.
assumptions: Both baskets contain the same goods.

provenance.description: Invented numbers explain a fixed budget. They do not describe measured prices.

distributional_effects.benefit: No benefit is assumed for the shopper in this fixed-budget comparison.
distributional_effects.cost: The shopper can buy fewer of the same baskets.
distributional_effects.time_horizon: Immediately after the basket price changes, while the budget remains fixed.
distributional_effects.conditions: The shopper does not substitute other goods or receive more income.

distributional_effects.benefit: The seller receives more money per basket sold.
distributional_effects.cost: The price change alone does not show whether profit increases. Costs or sales quantities may also change.
distributional_effects.time_horizon: The same selling period used for the price comparison.
distributional_effects.conditions: Revenue per basket and profit are different measures.

conditions_and_limits.title: Income can change too
conditions_and_limits.explanation: If the budget rises, the result depends on how much it rises relative to prices. This example holds the budget fixed.

conditions_and_limits.title: One product is not the whole economy
conditions_and_limits.explanation: A broad price measure combines many goods and services. A change in one basket cannot establish what happens to all prices.

misconceptions.belief: More money always means more purchasing power
misconceptions.correction: Purchasing power depends on prices as well as the amount of money.
misconceptions.explanation: A larger budget can still buy fewer goods if their prices rise sufficiently.

optional_depth.title: Money amount and buying capacity
optional_depth.explanation: A money amount describes the number of currency units. Buying capacity describes what those units can buy. A fair comparison states the goods, prices and period.

knowledge_checks.question: If the basket price returns to ₹100 and the budget stays at ₹500, how many baskets can you buy?
knowledge_checks.explanation: Divide ₹500 by ₹100 per basket. The comparison keeps the basket unchanged.

takeaways: Purchasing power describes what money can buy.
A fixed budget buys fewer unchanged goods when their price rises.
One basket example does not measure all inflation.
